title: AI Governance Readiness Scorecard for Professional Services
subtitle: Score your firm against the 4 gates that separate the 6% cutting costs from the 94% collecting subscriptions. Takes 6 minutes.

persona_selector.text: Which best describes your seat at the firm?

questions.text: Where does your client data actually live today?

answers.label: One unified system with clean records
6+ systems and nobody fully trusts any of them

questions.text: If a partner asked 'show me every active matter for client X across billing, documents, and email,' how long would that take?

answers.label: 10 to 30 minutes of digging across tools
Hours, and someone has to assemble it manually
We genuinely could not produce it

questions.text: What percentage of your intake forms collect structured data (dropdowns, defined fields) versus free-text?
When was the last time you audited duplicate or conflicting client records?

answers.label: Never, or we do not know how

low.headline: Your data is not ready for AI yet
low.text: Pointing an AI tool at fragmented data produces confident, wrong answers. The fix is not a smarter model, it is one source of truth before any pilot starts.
steps: Map every system holding client data this week and rank by trustworthiness
Pick the single workflow with the worst data sprawl and consolidate it into one system
Stand up a quarterly duplicate-record audit before evaluating any AI vendor

mid.headline: You have a foundation but the seams will leak
mid.text: Two-system syncs and half-structured intake work for humans because humans fill the gaps. AI will not. Tighten the seams before you scale.
steps: Convert remaining free-text intake fields into structured dropdowns within 30 days
Document exactly which fields sync between your two systems and which do not
Run a duplicate-record sweep and set a recurring 6-month cadence

high.headline: Your data foundation can carry an AI rollout
high.text: Unified records and fast retrieval are the leading indicator that AI pilots will produce measurable cost cuts rather than vibes.
steps: Document your data model and share it with any AI vendor you evaluate
Use this foundation to pilot one high-volume workflow this quarter
Add automated data quality alerts so the foundation does not erode

questions.text: Pick a recurring workflow (intake, billing, client reporting). Is it documented end-to-end with decision points?
If your most experienced senior left tomorrow, how much of their judgment is captured in writing?
How do exceptions and edge cases get handled today?

answers.label: We do not distinguish exceptions from normal work

low.headline: AI cannot automate what is not written down
low.text: Tribal knowledge is the single biggest reason AI pilots stall in professional services. The model needs the rules your seniors carry in their heads.
steps: Pick one recurring workflow and document it end-to-end with decision points this month
Interview your top 2 seniors and capture 20 representative edge cases in writing
Start a simple exception log so patterns surface within 90 days

mid.headline: You document the happy path but lose the edges
mid.text: Partial documentation gives AI enough to be dangerous. It will handle the 80% you wrote down and fail invisibly on the 20% you did not.
steps: Promote your best partial SOP into a versioned, reviewed document
Spend 2 hours capturing the exception patterns your team handles weekly
Add a quarterly review where exceptions become rules

high.headline: Your processes are ready for automation
high.text: Documented workflows with captured exceptions are exactly what AI agents need. You can move directly to pilot scoping.
steps: Identify the 3 documented workflows with the highest hour-cost and rank for automation
Convert your exception log into training examples for any AI tool you deploy
Keep the documentation review cadence so it does not decay

questions.text: Does your firm have a written policy for what AI tools staff can and cannot use with client data?
Who reviews AI-generated outputs before they reach a client?

answers.label: Whoever is closest to the matter
Outputs go out unreviewed, or we do not use AI yet

questions.text: Do you have an audit trail showing which staff used which AI tool on which matter?
How does your firm handle data residency and confidentiality for AI vendors?

answers.label: Vetted vendors with signed DPAs and known data locations

low.headline: You are one screenshot away from a client complaint
low.text: Staff are already using AI tools whether you sanctioned them or not. Without a written policy and audit trail, you cannot prove what happened when something goes wrong.
steps: Draft a one-page AI use policy this week covering allowed tools and prohibited data
Require all client-facing AI outputs to be reviewed by a named human
Inventory which AI vendors staff are currently using and where data flows

mid.headline: Your controls exist on paper but not in practice
mid.text: Verbal guidance and inconsistent review fail the moment a client asks how their data was handled. Governance only counts if it is enforced.
steps: Convert verbal guidance into a signed, versioned policy with quarterly attestation
Assign a single reviewer role for AI outputs with a documented checklist
Pick one AI tool and turn on full audit logging as a template for others

high.headline: Your governance posture is a competitive advantage
high.text: Most mid-market firms cannot answer governance questions in a sales cycle. You can. Use it.
steps: Publish a one-page AI governance summary you can share with clients on request
Run a quarterly review of audit logs to spot drift before it becomes incident
Renew DPAs annually and re-vet any vendor whose data residency changes

questions.text: How well do your current tools talk to each other?

answers.label: Connected via APIs or middleware, data flows automatically
Some integrations, mostly through Zapier or similar glue
A few manual exports between tools
Staff copy and paste between systems daily

questions.text: What percentage of repeatable tasks at your firm run without human touch today?
Who owns workflow automation at the firm?

answers.label: A named internal lead or external partner with a roadmap
Shared informally between ops and IT

low.headline: You have no chassis to put AI on
low.text: AI sitting next to manual copy-paste does not cut costs, it adds another tool to manage. You need an orchestration layer before AI can compound.
steps: Map the top 5 tasks where staff copy data between systems and estimate hours lost
Pilot one orchestration platform (n8n, Make, or similar) on the highest-volume task
Name a single owner for workflow automation with a 90-day roadmap

mid.headline: You have glue but not a system
mid.text: Zapier-style integrations get you started but break under volume and edge cases. AI plugged into brittle glue magnifies the brittleness.
steps: Audit your existing integrations for failure points and downtime over the last 90 days
Consolidate the top 3 workflows onto a more durable orchestration layer
Move workflow ownership from informal to a named lead with monthly review

high.headline: You are positioned to compound
high.text: With real orchestration and a named owner, every AI pilot you run stacks on the previous one. This is where the 20% cost cuts actually appear.
steps: Pick the workflow with the highest annual hours and design an AI augmentation
Set a quarterly target for percentage of repeatable tasks running untouched
Build a shared library of reusable automation components across workflows

questions.text: How much time and budget does the firm allocate to staff training on new tools each year?

answers.label: Dedicated budget and protected training hours
Ad hoc training when a tool launches
Staff figure it out on their own

questions.text: How does your firm typically run a software pilot?

answers.label: Defined success metrics, timeline, and go/no-go review
We have not piloted anything recently

questions.text: How aligned are partners on using AI to change how work gets done?

answers.label: Most are supportive, a few skeptics

questions.text: How do you measure whether a new tool actually reduced cost or time?

answers.label: Tracked before-and-after with specific hour and dollar metrics
Gut feel after a few months

low.headline: Your firm cannot absorb the change AI requires
low.text: AI does not fail because the technology is bad, it fails because nobody adopts it. Without training, pilot discipline, and measurement, every tool becomes shelfware.
steps: Allocate a small but protected training budget per staff member for the next 12 months
Define a written pilot template with success metrics and a 60-day review gate
Get partner alignment in writing before scoping any AI initiative

mid.headline: You can absorb change but not measure it
mid.text: Informal pilots and anecdotal feedback let leadership believe AI is working when it might not be. Discipline on measurement is what turns pilots into proof.
steps: Add specific hour and dollar baselines to every pilot before it starts
Schedule a formal go/no-go review at 60 and 90 days for any new tool
Document one win with hard numbers and use it to win over skeptical partners

high.headline: Your firm is built to compound AI wins
high.text: Training budget, disciplined pilots, partner alignment, and real measurement are the rare combination that turns AI from cost center into margin expansion.
steps: Build a 4-quarter AI roadmap with named owners and dollar targets per quarter
Publish internal case studies after each pilot to compound institutional learning
Tie a portion of partner comp or ops bonus to measured automation outcomes

cta.headline: Want a walkthrough of your score and the one workflow to fix first?
cta.description: Book a 30-minute strategy call. I will review your category scores live and identify the single highest-impact workflow your firm should automate next. No pitch, just a roadmap.
